steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between RNA and DNA  

1. Chemical composition  
   • Sugar: DNA contains deoxyribose (lacks an –OH on the 2′ carbon); RNA contains ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   • Bases: Both use adenine (A), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). DNA uniquely uses thymine (T); RNA substitutes uracil (U).  
   • Phosphate group: identical in both, linking 5′-3′ sugars to build the backbone.

2. Strand number & 3-D form  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the famous antiparallel double helix (B-form).  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded but can fold back on itself to create complex secondary/tertiary structures (hairpins, loops, pseudoknots). Some viruses do carry double-stranded RNA genomes.

3. Stability  
   • The extra 2′-OH in RNA makes it chemically less stable (prone to base-catalyzed hydrolysis) and more susceptible to nucleases.  
   • DNA’s absence of the 2′-OH plus helical shielding gives it higher chemical and enzymatic stability—ideal for long-term information storage.

4. Biological roles  
   DNA: primary, long-term storage of hereditary information.  
   RNA: versatile functional molecule. Major classes include  
      – mRNA: conveys genetic code from DNA to ribosome.  
      – rRNA: structural & catalytic core of ribosomes.  
      – tRNA: adapters that bring amino acids during translation.  
      – snRNA, snoRNA, miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.: regulation, processing, defense, scaffolding.  
   In some RNA viruses (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2), RNA itself is the genetic material.

5. Cellular location  
   • Eukaryotes: DNA resides mainly in the nucleus (plus mitochondria/chloroplasts). RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions largely in the cytoplasm and other compartments.  
   • Prokaryotes: both DNA and RNA are in the cytoplasm/nucleoid, but roles remain distinct.

6. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA replicates via DNA polymerases, producing an identical DNA copy.  
   • RNA is made by transcription of DNA using RNA polymerase, producing a complementary RNA strand; RNA isn’t typically copied back to DNA except by specialized enzymes (reverse transcriptase).

7. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA has extensive proofreading and repair pathways because mutations affect heredity.  
   • RNA usually lacks such robust repair; errors generally have transient effects because RNA molecules are short-lived.

8. Experimental handling  
   • DNA is easier to isolate and store; it survives heat and pH extremes better.  
   • RNA work demands stringent RNase-free conditions and quick processing to avoid degradation.

Summary  
DNA = durable, double-stranded repository of genetic blueprints.  
RNA = more fragile, usually single-stranded, multifunctional molecule that reads, interprets, and sometimes stores genetic information, as well as catalyzes and regulates cellular processes.
